Binghamton.wildlife_intro:
Binghamton keeps our crew busy with Norway rats near the river wards, raccoons and squirrels in hillside attics, and groundhogs under hillside porches and retaining walls. Susquehanna River  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Binghamton. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Binghamton jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Endicott.wildlife_intro:
Endicott is the Triple Cities' factory village — Endicott Johnson's shoe plants and IBM's birthplace built rows of worker housing along the Susquehanna, much of it still standing and still occupied. Those pre-war homes and doubles are the wildlife story: squirrels and raccoons in aging attics, bats in the eaves of the older streets, and Norway rats around the former industrial ground and oldest blocks. The river flats behind the village keep skunks in the yards.

Factory housing was built fast and alike, so Endicott's entries repeat street after street: the same soffit detail, the same chimney flashing, failing on the same schedule. Our crew inspects Endicott homes against that pattern, removes the animals, and seals the full set of likely openings. River humidity is hard on foundations here too, so cellars get checked on every rat or skunk call.

Tight lots mean Johnson City animals commute across fences and shared driveways, and a porch void on one property shelters animals feeding on three others. Our crew inspects Johnson City homes with the block in view, removes the animals, and seals or screens the entries — porch screening earns its keep here as much as roofline work, because the village's skunk traffic is a ground-level problem first.

Chenango.wildlife_intro:

Suburban streets near the city get squirrels and raccoons in postwar attics; the rural north gets groundhogs on the farm lots, skunks under outbuildings, and bats in older farmhouses. The river corridor and its tributary creeks move animals through the whole town.

Chenango's long town shape means our crew scopes by address, not by town average: what a house near the Binghamton line needs and what a farmhouse near Chenango Forks needs share only the inspection. We remove the animals, seal the dwellings, and screen the outbuilding voids on rural properties — spring groundhog emergence and the fall squirrel push are the town's two busy seasons at both ends.
